how: From one live report for z-ai/glm-5.3-flash, fetched on 19 November 2026 at 21:57 UTC with no account key, through a Tor of our own, by guest/near's cloak-near-probe (nonce 1806ef297c5cce6cfa907354cda27e78f8c4746d01d69c01ab56ac168714c947, gateway TLS key SHA-256 73862c254372091cc6895b900111503860694f8916ebf0c63b18d245ba8ba5ad). Before these values were written, that report passed every other check in guest/near, for the gateway and each of its 3 model instances: Intel's quote check (UpToDate, collateral fetched from Intel through Tor), report data with the TLS binding and the nonce, the echoed nonce and TLS key, the RTMR3 replay and MRCONFIGID against the compose file. MRTD, RTMR0-2 and MRCONFIGID are read from the verified quotes; app_id, key_provider, mr_kms and os_image_hash are the payloads of those RTMR3 events, in hex. The model sets are every distinct set among that report's instances, in the report's order. Later on 19 November 2026 the model sets were changed to carry compose_sha256_without_label in place of mrconfigid, because every model server's compose file names its own host once, as INSTANCE_LABEL=gpu and digits: it is the SHA-256 of the instance's compose file exactly as presented (the app_compose text its MRCONFIGID binds) with those digits dropped, and nothing else. The three were computed from that report's three composes (whole SHA-256 c900dc73..., e8416a02... and fb81c6f2..., labels gpu03, gpu13 and gpu23); none becomes the same as another once the label is dropped, so all three sets stay. A second report for z-ai/glm-5.3-flash, fetched the same way at 00:22 UTC on 20 November (nonce 2a7e2ceea9654d9d1df90cac67839e8bc47c527559f942824dc4bf42ebaa07be, the same gateway TLS key), listed the same three instances with the same composes, and with these pins passed every check in guest/near at its fetch time, Intel Trust Authority's verdict on the GPUs included. The gateway set still pins MRCONFIGID, the whole compose hash: the gateway's compose has no label. Not pinned: a second Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B server, instance 7bb9af0ac5b0e22dde3903218f58e56f743164a1, label gpu04, compose SHA-256 e3902667a26282dd8b4015a901848c521b20243a155a457148f88acf48a45959, without the label f2b223e76cab20967708301fe4191f0ecefdf9be92cfd3b77e19b4fa68fba0de, seen on 19 November beside instance a8a25faab3ef437d2da809382e05e59e3c55a0f5. Its compose differs from the gpu23 one in the label and in its telemetry address (telemetry.infra.near.ai in place of telemetry-stg.infra.near.ai), so its set would be a fourth one. It is the fourth model set: on 20 November 2026 at about 00:45 UTC a fresh keyless report for Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B, through a Tor of our own, was refused by cloak-near-probe only at the pin step, the last one, naming this server's MRTD, OS image and compose hash without the label; every earlier step (Intel's quote check, report data, the echoed nonce and TLS key, the RTMR3 replay, MRCONFIGID against the compose, one key, distinct instances) had passed for it. Its other values are the gpu23 set's. The set was added after its compose was read against the gpu23 one, and the same probe then passed. The one Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B instance seen earlier that day, in four reports over nine minutes, is instance a8a25faab3ef437d2da809382e05e59e3c55a0f5, which the first report lists too, with the same set. Nothing here is signed by NEAR: NEAR publishes no list of expected values for its own servers, so these are what its servers presented that day.
